pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 5–6 years

- **Topic:** Testing Push & Pull Designs

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum (England)):** NOTE HONESTLY: there is NO forces content at Key Stage 1 — 'pushes and pulls' / forces first appear at Year 3 (KS2) and the 'forces as pushes or pulls' framing only at KS3. What KS1 DOES provide, and what this topic exercises, is the statutory 'Working scientifically' skill set for Years 1–2 (taught through other content): 'performing simple tests', 'gathering and recording data to help in answering questions', and 'using their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions' (plus 'asking simple questions'). So the UK anchor here is the ENQUIRY skill, not the forces content. (Statutory wording verified by fetch of gov.uk KS1 science programme of study.)

- **Standards — US (NGSS K-PS2-2):** This topic, essentially verbatim: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-2].' Clarification: problems such as making an object move a distance, follow a path, or knock down others; solutions such as a ramp to increase speed or a structure to make it turn. Assessment boundary: [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-2]. SEP 'Analyzing and Interpreting Data' (K–2: collect, record and share observations) — element: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-2, K-2-ETS1-3, K-PS2-2].' DCIs PS2.A (pushes/pulls have different strengths and directions; can change speed/direction, start/stop) and ETS1.A (a situation people want to change can be approached as an engineering problem with many acceptable solutions). (Verified by fetch of nextgenscience.org K-PS2-2.)

- **Operational details:** This is a PROCEDURAL (engineering-practice) topic, not a new force concept — it sits on top of the prerequisite 'Pushes & Pulls' (stronger/weaker, different directions change an object's speed or direction). The child sets a concrete GOAL (make the marble reach the bear, follow a path, or knock down the cups), uses or builds a simple design (a ramp, a launcher, a barrier), TESTS it, collects simple data on whether it met the goal (a mark where it stopped, a hit/miss tally, a photo), ANALYSES that record to decide if the design works as intended, then SUGGESTS a modification (steeper ramp, harder push, a wall to turn it) and re-tests. The whole point is the test–observe–record–judge–improve loop, kept concrete: the evidence, not the wish, decides whether it worked.

Best taught by anchoring a clear, observable success criterion first, predicting before each test, recording the result in a child-readable way BEFORE judging it, and changing only one thing between tries so the comparison means something — the seed of fair testing without the formal language. Talk is the main tool: 'How do you know it worked?' presses for evidence.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier A (concrete / observational, ≈5–6; kindergarten / Year 1, pre- and early-readers). The child works entirely with real objects they can push, pull, build and watch — no measurement formalism, no variable-control vocabulary, no symbols. The cognitive stretch is small but real: judging a design against an OBSERVED outcome ('did it do what we wanted?') rather than against what they hoped or how fun it was. Keep everything hands-on, picture-and-talk based, one change at a time.
bestPractices: Set a concrete, observable GOAL with the child first (reach the bear / knock down the cups / make it curve round) so 'works as intended' can be checked against what happened, not against hopes or how fun it was.
Predict, then test: have the child say or point to what they think will happen before each release, so the test becomes a question being answered, not just play.
Record the outcome BEFORE judging it — mark where the marble stopped, drop a hit/miss token, take a photo — giving a child-readable trace they can look back at to decide if the design worked.
Change only ONE thing between tries (steeper ramp OR harder push) and re-test, comparing the two records — fair-testing logic planted without the vocabulary.

Keep it a push/pull story (the substantive idea underneath): a stronger push sends it further/faster, a steeper ramp speeds it up, a wall or barrier turns it — and stay within the assessment boundary by varying push strength or ramp, not friction.
Use talk as the main analysis tool: ask 'How do you know it worked?' and 'What one thing could we change?' to press for evidence-based reasoning at a level a 5-year-old can manage.
Distinguish 'it met the goal' from 'that was fun' explicitly — young children readily conflate enjoyment or intention with success.
keyRepresentations: A ramp-and-marble (or simple launcher) test rig with a clearly marked GOAL/target
A child-readable results record: a mark on the track where the marble stopped each try, or a hit/miss tally of tokens/stickers
A before/after design comparison: low ramp vs high ramp, gentle vs hard push, with the two outcomes side by side
A picture 'goal card' showing the intended outcome (reach the bear / knock the cups / follow the curved path)
Push/pull arrows on the object linking the action to the change in speed or direction (ties back to the prerequisite)
commonMisconceptions: Judging that the design 'worked' by intention or enjoyment ('I wanted it to, so it did' / 'it was fun, so it worked') rather than by the observed outcome against the goal.
Treating the goal vaguely so success can't be checked — no concrete, observable success criterion was set.
Changing several things at once between tries, so the child can't tell which change made the difference (emergent fair-testing gap at this age).
Expecting one try to settle it — not yet repeating the test or noticing run-to-run variation.

Carrying the 'motion needs a continuous force' intuition from Pushes & Pulls — thinking the object keeps a push 'inside it' (the impetus idea seeded young; keep the focus on the design test, not on explaining why it eventually stops, which is outside the K assessment boundary anyway).
Thinking a design that failed the goal is simply 'broken' rather than something to modify and improve (missing the iterate-and-improve idea).

learn.summary: For 5–6 year olds, the learning goal is a hands-on engineering-enquiry loop: set an observable goal, predict, test, record the outcome, read the record to judge whether the design met the goal, change ONE thing, and re-test. The teaching objective is first-hand building and testing with real ramps, marbles, launchers and targets, where the recorded evidence (not the child's wish or how fun it was) decides success — and a design that missed the goal is something to improve, not simply 'broken'. A screen 'design-test bench' is a strong proxy for the data-and-judgment logic but cannot provide the haptic build-and-test experience, so it belongs alongside real apparatus. Stay within the K-PS2-2 assessment boundary by changing speed with push strength or ramp height, and direction with push direction or a block/wall/curved track that turns the marble, not friction. The UK anchor is the Working Scientifically enquiry skill, not forces content, which is not in KS1.

activities.title: Real ramp-and-marble design test (primary hands-on investigation)
feedback: If the child re-rolls identically after an overshoot or undershoot, ask 'did it go too far or not far enough?' then 'what one thing could make it go a bit less/more?' to tie the change to the observation.
If several things change at once (marble, ramp height and push together), reset and change only ONE so the effect of that change is clear.
If the child pushes HARDER after an overshoot, revisit that a gentler push or lower ramp gives a shorter roll, connecting how hard the push is to how far it travels.

If the child treats a design that missed the goal as simply 'broken', reframe it: the aim is to change one thing and try again to get closer — missing the goal tells us what to improve, not that the test failed.
Explicitly separate 'it met the goal' from 'that was fun' — praise meeting the goal distinctly, since young children readily conflate enjoyment or intention with success.
Press 'How do you know it worked?' and 'What one thing could we change?' so the child points to the marks/tokens as evidence.
activities.rationale: The learning IS the test–observe–record–judge–improve loop, and at this age it should be felt and messy: building a real ramp, feeling the push, watching a real marble, marking where it stopped and deciding together. Recording before judging gives a child-readable trace, one-change-at-a-time plants fair-testing logic without formal vocabulary, and re-testing after a miss builds the iterate-and-improve habit. Talk is the main analysis tool at a level a 5-year-old can manage.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-PS2-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-2].' Clarification gives marble-to-a-goal problems and ramp/turn-structure solutions; assessment boundary excludes friction as a mechanism; SEP element '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-2, K-2-ETS1-3, K-PS2-2]'; DCIs PS2.A (pushes/pulls strengths and directions change speed/direction) and ETS1.A (engineering problems have many acceptable solutions).

DfE England National Curriculum: forces are NOT in the Key Stage 1 programme of study (forces first appear at Year 3); KS1 'Working scientifically' (Years 1–2) statutorily requires 'performing simple tests', 'gathering and recording data to help in answering questions', and 'using their observations and ideas to suggest answers to questions' — the enquiry skills this topic exercises.

Young children tend to judge whether something 'worked' by intention or enjoyment rather than by evidence; primary enquiry teaching should name the enquiry type honestly, base predictions/conclusions on the observed data, take repeated tries, and press 'how do you know?' to connect claim to evidence.
learnerActions: Agree a concrete, observable goal together first, e.g. make the marble reach the teddy, knock down the cups, or follow a curved path round a barrier.
Before each release, say or point to what you think will happen (predict).
Roll the marble, then BEFORE deciding if it worked, record the outcome: mark on the mat/track where the marble stopped, or drop a hit/miss token or sticker onto a results strip.

Change only ONE thing between tries (higher OR lower ramp, harder OR gentler push, or, for a turning goal, moving a block/wall that steers the marble), re-test, and place the new record next to the last one.
Look back along the row of recorded stops and decide: did the design meet the goal? Pick the next change the records point to, and re-test to confirm.
Say out loud how you know it worked, using the marks and tokens as evidence.
activities.intendedInsight: A design 'works as intended' when the recorded outcome meets the agreed goal — the evidence decides, not what you hoped or how fun it was; changing one thing at a time lets you see what each change did, and a miss is something to change and try again.

activities.title: Screen 'design-test bench' (digital companion for the data-judgment logic)
feedback: Separate 'met the goal' feedback from 'fun' feedback.
Use picture and audio prompts, no required reading, since learners are pre- and early-readers.
If a child wants to change two things, surface the 'change one thing' lock so the comparison stays meaningful.
Vary ramp height, push strength or push direction, or add a wall/bumper that turns the marble — keep within the assessment boundary by not introducing friction as the mechanism.
activities.rationale: A coded bench can run tests, leave a persistent visual record of each outcome, and let the child read that record to judge the goal and choose a change — helping make 'analyze data to determine if it works as intended' concrete via a live recompute plus an accumulating results strip. A persistent, readable record supports the data-judgment insight; it does not replace the haptic build-and-test experience, so use it alongside real apparatus.
sourceClaims: NGSS K-PS2-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-2].' Clarification gives marble-to-a-goal problems and ramp/turn-structure solutions; assessment boundary excludes friction as a mechanism; SEP element '[curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-PS1-2, K-2-ETS1-3, K-PS2-2]'; DCIs PS2.A (pushes/pulls strengths and directions change speed/direction) and ETS1.A (engineering problems have many acceptable solutions).
learnerActions: Set ONE thing on the ramp/launcher: drag the ramp height OR pull back a push slider, or, for the curve-path goal, place a wall/bumper that turns the marble (shown from above).
Tap to predict what will happen, then release the marble toward the goal target (reach the bear / knock cups / curve path).
Watch the bench leave a stop-mark where the marble stopped and drop a hit/miss token onto a results strip at the bottom.

After a few tries, read the filled results strip at a glance and see what it actually shows — for a reach-the-target goal, tries that are too gentle or too low may fall short, while tries that are too hard or too high may roll past.

Pick the change the evidence points to (higher ramp or harder push when it fell short; lower ramp or gentler push when it rolled past; move the wall when it went the wrong way) and re-test to confirm; the 'change one thing' lock greys out a second change until the first is tested.
activities.intendedInsight: Watching recorded outcomes accumulate and reading that strip to make a decision shows that the recorded data, not the wish, tells you whether the design works — and what one change to try next.

activities.title: Labelled scene vocabulary primer (reference layer)
feedback: Use this as a reference and vocabulary layer paired with the bench or the real rig, not on its own.
Reinforce the push/pull words that tie back to the prerequisite 'Pushes & Pulls' (stronger/weaker, different directions).
activities.rationale: A static labelled scene with tap-to-reveal naming is a useful vocabulary primer. Because nothing runs or records, it names the parts rather than eliciting the test-and-judge practice, so it is a supporting reference used alongside an activity where the child actually tests and records.
learnerActions: Tap parts of a static scene (ramp, marble, push arrow, goal) to reveal naming: 'this is a push', 'this is the ramp', 'this is our goal'.
Tap the ramp to reveal 'a ramp can make it go faster'; tap the goal to reveal the reflective prompt 'did the marble reach it?'
Lift a flap on 'how could we make it go further?' to reveal 'start it higher up — make the ramp higher'.
activities.intendedInsight: Reinforces the prerequisite push/pull words and names the parts of the test setup so the enquiry vocabulary is in place.

activities.title: Picture-and-audio judgment check (light consolidation)
feedback: Keep all steps image/audio-based with minimal text for pre- and early-readers.
Use simple illustrations that show clearly different stopping points; no exact measurements are needed.

Treat this as a companion check that recognises a conclusion; it does not itself elicit the child generating and reading their own data, so pair it with the hands-on testing rather than using it alone.
activities.rationale: Picture-driven steps can consolidate the judgment after hands-on testing. At 5–6 these lean on adult-read or audio prompts and check recognition of a conclusion rather than independent data generation, so they supplement, not replace, the construction activity.
learnerActions: Answer an image-based question: 'Did the marble reach the bear? yes/no'.
Compare two pictures that each show where the marble stopped, and pick which ramp made it go further by looking at the stopping points.
Put the test steps in order: predict → test → look → decide.
activities.intendedInsight: Consolidates judging a design against an observed outcome and the order of the test loop, after the child has done real testing.

constraints: UK honesty note: forces are NOT in the KS1 programme of study (they first appear at Year 3; the 'forces as pushes or pulls' framing at KS3). The KS1 anchor is the statutory 'Working scientifically' enquiry skill set, not forces content.
Assessment boundary (K-PS2-2): do [curriculum wording omitted; reference K-PS2-2]; vary push strength, push direction or ramp height, or add a block/wall/curved track that turns the marble, instead.
Tier A concrete/observational level: real objects only, no measurement formalism, no variable-control vocabulary, no symbols; keep everything hands-on, picture-and-talk based, one change at a time.
The screen bench is a proxy for the data-judgment logic and cannot provide the haptic build-and-test experience; use it alongside real apparatus, not as a replacement.

The labelled scene names the parts and vocabulary; the picture-and-audio check recognises a conclusion rather than eliciting the child's own generated data. Neither substitutes for the hands-on build-test-record loop, though each can support it.
Keep the focus on the design test, not on explaining WHY the marble eventually stops (impetus/continuous-force intuition) — that is outside the K assessment boundary.
Distinguish 'it met the goal' from 'that was fun' explicitly; young children readily conflate enjoyment or intention with success.
Repeat tries rather than expecting one try to settle it, and notice run-to-run variation.
Treat a design that missed the goal as something to change and re-test, not as simply 'broken' — the point is to iterate and improve.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched this session. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The NGSS K-PS2-2 and DfE sources are marked verified in the row; the PSTT/Ogden Trust claim about young children judging success by intention/enjoyment is marked verified:false (synthesised via prior research, not fetched). It is used because it directly supports the 'judge by evidence' principle, but treat it as plausible guidance, not established fact.

The original row asserted the results strip makes the practice concrete 'in a way no static or spoken medium can' and that 'live recompute plus a persistent record is exactly what a static page or a talk cannot give'. These comparative-necessity claims are softened: a persistent, readable record supports the data-judgment insight, but static and spoken media can still teach aspects of the loop; catalog ratings do not establish universal necessity.

The original 3D 'adds nothing / clarifies nothing' and conversation 'cannot be the vehicle' framings were removed as over-strong universal claims; the retained points are only that a flat side-view representation suffices for this data-and-judgment goal and that talk prompts support but need not carry the whole test experience.

Force/motion check: the assessment's 'push harder to fix an overshoot' is correctly flagged as an error — a gentler push or lower ramp gives a shorter roll. This is preserved as corrective feedback in activity 1.

The simulated bench outcomes (which ramp heights/push strengths reach the target) are design assumptions, not empirically tested; activity 2 wording was made non-deterministic so the child reads whatever the record actually shows.
The misconception that a failed design is simply 'broken' rather than improvable is covered explicitly in both the summary and activity 1 feedback.

probeDeeper: Did the marble go too far, or not far enough? How could you tell?
What one thing did you change, and what happened when you tried again?
If it went way too far, would you push harder or gentler next time? Why?
How do you know your change made it better?
assess.correctAnswer: Rolls the marble and watches whether it overshoots, stops short, or lands on the target, then makes a purposeful change based on what happened — e.g. lower the ramp (or start gentler) if it overshoots, raise it if it stops short — and tries again, judging success by whether the marble lands closer. Links the change to the observed result (too far -> less push / lower ramp).

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It didn't work, so I'll just try again the same way.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Ask 'did it go too far or not far enough?' then 'what could make it go a bit less/more?' — tie the change to the observation.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Repeats the attempt identically without adjusting after an overshoot or undershoot.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'To get it closer I'll change lots of things at once.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Change ONE thing and re-test so the effect of that change is clear.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Swaps the marble, ramp height and push together, so it's impossible to tell what helped.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'It overshot, so I need to push HARDER to fix it.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Revisit that a gentler push / lower ramp gives a shorter roll; connect the force to how far it travels.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Makes the change that worsens the result (more push when it already went too far).

responseLevels.gap: Re-rolls without adjusting, or changes things at random / all at once; can't say whether the marble met the target.
responseLevels.full: Reads the outcome (too far / too short), makes ONE purposeful change in the right direction (gentler/lower if it overshot), re-tests, and judges improvement by the marble landing closer — connecting the design change to the observed effect.
responseLevels.partial: Notices whether the marble reached the target and makes a change, but the change isn't clearly linked to the result (or several things change at once) — tests without using what was observed to steer the next try.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here is a little ramp and a marble. We want the marble to roll across the mat and STOP on the target circle. Have a go at making that happen. Try it a few times, watch what the marble does, then change something to get it closer to the target — and tell me what you changed and why.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watch the child. The discriminator is whether the change is DATA-DRIVEN — chosen because of what the marble just did (overshot -> make it gentler) — versus random fiddling or changing everything at once. A child who re-rolls the same way, or makes a change unrelated to the outcome (moves the target, or changes marble AND ramp AND push together), shows they aren't reading the result to improve the design.
